analysis.one_liner: Speeds approval of cheaper generic drugs by curbing brand-name drug companies' delay petitions.
analysis.headline: Introduced in October 2025 with a bipartisan sponsor team, the bill has sat in the Senate health committee for over a month with no hearing, no vote, and only two cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Brand-name drug companies can file "citizen petitions" with the FDA — formal requests asking the agency to take action — and some are filed mainly to stall approval of cheaper generic or biosimilar copies of their drugs, sometimes for years. This bill tells the FDA what warning signs to look for when deciding a petition's main purpose is delay, such as serial petitions, filings right before an approval date, or demands for extra testing. It also requires a company to file a petition before it can sue the FDA to block a generic, gives it 180 days after learning relevant facts to file, and lets courts dismiss lawsuits that skip those steps.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and households that buy prescription drugs, because faster generic and biosimilar approval brings lower-priced competition to market sooner. Generic and biosimilar manufacturers also gain a clearer, faster path to approval.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients who pay for prescription drugs

how_it_helps.text: Directs the FDA to weigh factors like serial petitions, petitions filed close to an expected approval date, and demands for more onerous testing when deciding whether a petition was filed primarily to delay a generic or biosimilar application [S2].

Requires anyone seeking to block a generic or biosimilar approval in court to first file a petition with the FDA, and to do so within 180 days of learning the relevant information; courts must dismiss suits that skip these steps [S2].
Narrows exceptions to the existing process under which the FDA must respond to petitions within 150 days or approve the application anyway [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers lose a legal tool that extends the period they can charge monopoly prices after patents expire. Some petitions raising genuine safety concerns could face a tighter 180-day deadline, and public-interest groups could find it harder to sue the FDA directly without first going through the petition process.

drawbacks.text: The mandatory petition-before-lawsuit rule and the 180-day filing deadline could shut out patient groups and public-interest organizations that raise legitimate safety questions but lack the resources to file quickly or exhaust the full process first [S2].
Courts must dismiss untimely suits "with prejudice," meaning a petition that misses the 180-day window cannot bring the issue back, even if the underlying concern is valid [S2].

The bill adds new judgment calls for FDA staff about a petitioner's intent and knowledge, which could invite litigation over how the factors are applied and modestly increase the agency's administrative workload [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is faster access to lower-priced generics and biosimilars, which is where most prescription drug savings for consumers come from. The main cost is that some legitimate petitions, including from patient advocates rather than drug companies, will face tighter deadlines and an extra procedural step before court. On balance the bill targets a well-documented delay tactic while leaving the petition process itself available, but the dismissal-with-prejudice penalty is unforgiving and the benefit depends on FDA actually using its new authority.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate health committee in mid-October 2025, and nothing has happened since — no hearing, no vote, just two cosponsors.

narrative.text: Sen. Shaheen introduced the bill on October 16, 2025, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day [S4].
It has two cosponsors, one Republican and one Democrat, and the HELP committee has taken no further action on it [S1].
The bill would amend the FDA's citizen-petition process for generic and biosimilar applications, targeting petitions filed primarily to delay approval [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has acted, so the status quo holds: brand-name drug makers keep their current delay tools while the bill sits in committee, and consumers keep paying brand-name prices longer than they otherwise might.

for.name: Sen. Jeanne Shaheen
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Hampshire, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the HELP committee

for.name: Sen. Susan Collins
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill's introduction and cosponsored it

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat and a Republican introduced the bill together, with one cosponsor from each party; no opposition has been recorded, but only 2 of 100 senators have signed on so far.

industries.note: These companies use citizen petitions and follow-on lawsuits to stretch the period they can charge monopoly prices after patents expire. The bill makes those delay tactics harder by letting FDA weigh intent factors and requiring exhaustion before suit.
Faster approval of generic and biosimilar applications gets their products to market sooner, and their interest in quicker approvals runs alongside patients' interest in lower prices.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to the Senate HELP Committee with only a handful of cosponsors and no scheduled hearing rarely reach the floor, and prior versions of this measure have stalled in committee in earlier Congresses. Unless the committee schedules action or the bill is attached to a larger drug-pricing package, it is likely to expire at the end of this Congress without a vote.
